what: Decision Matrix helps you choose between several options in a fair, clear way. You list the options as columns and the things that matter as rows, give each criterion an importance, and score every option from 0 to 10.

It calculates a weighted score out of 10 for each option, ranks them with a bar chart, and runs a sensitivity check that tells you which change in importance would make a different option win, so you know how solid the result is.
Ready-made templates help you start, and your decisions are saved privately in your browser, with CSV, backup and print.
uses: Compare models on price, battery, camera and more.
Weigh pay against growth, commute and work-life balance.
Compare homes or neighbourhoods on cost, safety and commute.
Score vendors on price, quality, delivery and service.
Agree on criteria first, then score together.
Compare courses and schools on what matters to you.
tutorial: Pick a template and press Use template, or press New for a blank matrix. Give the decision a name.
Type the option names in the column headers. Use + Add option for more, × to remove.
Type what matters in the first column. Use + Add criterion for more.
Choose 1 (nice to have) to 5 (essential) for each criterion, or switch to Percentages.
Give each option 0 (very poor) to 10 (excellent) for each criterion. 10 always means best for you, so a cheap option scores high on price.
See the winner, ranking and bar chart, and read the sensitivity check.
Your work saves automatically. Print it, download a CSV, or back up all decisions to a file.
features: A clear weighted average out of 10 for each option.
Importance 1–5 or percentages that add to 100%.
Bars make the gap between options easy to see.
Shows which weight change would flip the winner.
Phone, job offer, place to live, laptop, supplier.
Keep, copy and switch between saved decisions.
Open in a spreadsheet or print a one-page summary.

example.title: Example: two phones
example.text: Phone A scores 8 for price, 6 for camera and 7 for battery; Phone B scores 6, 9 and 8. With importance 5 for price, 3 for camera and 4 for battery, Phone A gets (40 + 18 + 28) ÷ 12 = 7.17 and Phone B gets (30 + 27 + 32) ÷ 12 = 7.42, so Phone B wins by 0.25. The sensitivity check says lowering camera's importance from 3 to 1 would make Phone A win.

tips: Agree on the criteria and their importance before you score, so you are not tempted to tweak them to get the answer you want.
Keep criteria separate; do not count the same thing twice under two names.
If two options are very close, the matrix is telling you both are fine. Go with your gut or the cheaper one.
Use Copy to try a different set of weights without losing the original.
Back up your decisions before clearing your browser.
problems: It says empty scores count as 0
Fill in every score, or the options with gaps will look worse than they are.
My percentages do not add to 100%
The tool still works by scaling them, but adjust them so the total shows 100%.
The table is cut off on my phone
Swipe sideways inside the table to see the other options.
They are stored in this browser only. Restore your latest backup file with Restore backup.
